sections.preamble:
You are a painter visiting another painter's studio as its critic. The studio is the folder you are in. You see the painting with the look tool and read the painter's journal and its note to you with the read tool. You don't paint.

You are not being evaluated in a quantifiable way.

toolsAdded.name: look
toolsAdded.description: Look at the canvas as it is now. Without options: the whole canvas, scaled down. crop: "x0,y0,x1,y1" in canvas units (two opposite corners), at full detail up to 1200 pixels a side; larger crops are scaled down. The reply gives the scale in pixels per canvas unit. mask: a global mask's name (or several, comma-separated), shown as outlines and a light fill over the view. mode: "value" (the picture in grays, its lightness alone, in the gallery light), "squint", "edges" (the picture's edges drawn over a dim gray of it: orange where an edge is hard, blue where it is soft, brighter the more the lightness changes across it; hard and soft as they read at the size of the image the look returns), "mirror", "relief" (a raking light on the paint's ridges and furrows), "gallery" (the light the picture hangs in) or several, comma-separated. light: "azimuth,elevation" in degrees for the relief light (default "135,25", from the upper left). size: the long side in pixels. grid: true, or a spacing in canvas units. survey: true surveys the whole canvas at full detail, as several tiles (with mode, not crop or size); a partial reply lists remaining tiles to read in separate turns. compare: the path of an earlier look, shown left of the current view; supply matching crop, mode and light options explicitly. ref: the path of a picture of the motif in this studio (a photograph, a study), fitted to the canvas's shape (scaled to cover it and centered, so a picture of another shape loses its edges) and shown left of the same view of the canvas: the same crop, size, mode and grid, as a picture pinned beside the easel. hold: the name of a knife (what is on it) or a pile (a fresh load), with at: "x,y" (canvas units): the loaded knife held up to the canvas there, its paint thick on the blade (crop sets the passage). Supports mode value, squint, relief or gallery and light; size, grid and mirror are unavailable with hold. It shows the paint on the knife, not how it would look laid. palette: true shows the palette board instead: each pile knifed out thick and smeared thin across a black stripe.

scratch.description: true: the scratch canvas beside the painting instead of the painting. It is set up as the painting's canvas was, with its own palette, brushes and variables, and its own log; nothing done there reaches the painting. It keeps its own clock: time spent or waited there doesn't pass for the painting.

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

content.text:
The painter has asked you to visit while it works, and you've come to see the painting.

Look at it as closely as you like: the whole canvas, detail crops, the value, squint, mirror, relief and gallery views and the palette. Read the painter's journal, notes/journal.md, and its note to you, notes/to_critic.md.

The painter's journal has no `Open passages:` list yet.

Then tell the painter what you would fix and why, as one painter talking to another: what you see, what it does to the picture and what you would do about it. Say which passage, if any, you would take up first, whether or not it is on the painter's list. Your last message is what the painter gets. The painter reads it as soon as you finish, and it is saved in the studio as notes/critic.md. The painter decides what to do with it.

content.text:
- day 1, 09:00: ## Sitting 1 — plan
  Concept 4: autumn woodland stream falling over mossy rocks, small waterfall, white birches, gold/rust foliage reflected in pool.
  Canvas: 480 mm wide, aspect 0.8 (W 1000, H 1250), linen 18x15, ground lead white 10 + yellow ochre 0.4 + raw umber 0.15, 120 µm knife, texture 0.25 (warm cream).
  Composition (portrait): glow in the back woods upper left-center (~x380,y300), canopy gold/rust across the top with sky gaps; ledge ~y585 across middle; falls x~400–560 dropping to ~y780 in two strands split by a rock; pool y 780–1250 with vertical reflections of canopy and birches, foam at base; two birches on right bank (x~760, ~870), a slimmer one left behind the rocks; mossy rock lower left foreground, floating leaves.
  Values: lights = falls, foam, birches, glow; darks = rock under the lip, pool depths near banks, deep woods at edges; mids = foliage, moss.
  Method (wet-on-wet): a thin oily wet film first, then back to front, dark before light, all into open paint within the day: glow/back woods → canopy masses → rocks/ledge (knife) → pool base + vertical reflection pulls + horizontal passes → falls pulled down + foam → birches (thick light over wet dark) → moss lights, leaves, twigs, highlights.
  Palette: lead white; gold = chrome yellow + ochre (+white); rust = red earth + ochre + touch vermilion; darks = Prussian + red earth + umber; moss = green earth + chrome + ochre, Prussian + chrome + ochre; water = white + cobalt; birch shadow = white + smalt + umber.
- day 1, 09:00: Scratch trials 1 (dry cream ground, all into open paint, day 1 morning):
  - Palette board: dark (Prussian 1, red earth 2, umber 2) = neutral charcoal; pool_dark (Prussian 1, umber 2, green earth 1) = slate navy, too blue for a woodland pool; birch_shadow (white 4, smalt 1, umber .5) nearly white — smalt is weak; water_white (white 6, cobalt .4) nearly white.
  - Thick white (flat 14, lay 4, load 1) over WET dark body paint: lays clean and opaque, little pickup. Flat brushes at default orient lay a narrow mark (~half width); use orient="across" for full width.
  - Knife (width 18–40) loaded fully, pressure 0.3–0.6: runs out after ~75 units; leaves a broken, weave-gridded texture, mechanical over a big area.
  - Graded `piles` (glow ↔ deepwood) mix into khaki in the middle. blend() inside a hard rect leaves a crisp box and lifts paint (paler). Use soft, larger masks.
  - Foliage: stipple width 5–7 at cov 1.2 = a dense ball of uniform dots; fan touches and filbert 8 dabs = tiny dots at this scale. Need larger marks / masses first.
  - Pool: dark base, then vertical gold/rust strokes, then blend(angle=pi/2) over a softened rect = convincing soft vertical reflections. A "wiped" flat (wipe .95) for horizontal passes still laid stripes of olive — use blend with a clean blender instead.
  - Falls: parallel filbert gestures = noodles. A gray-blue sheet + dry flat streaks + vertical blend = soft but opaque, bell-shaped mask shows. Filbert touches for foam = flat angular chips (bad).
- day 1, 09:00: Scratch trials 2 (fresh scratch, all wet):
  - FALLS recipe that read as water: rock dark laid solid (broad, cov 3, clip, fill=true); then fallgray (white 3, cobalt .3, umber .4, ochre .1) in broken vertical flat-14 strokes, load .25–.4, pressure .25–.45→.1, orient across; then ONE blend pass angle pi/2 over a softened mask (veils it into streaks); then water_white (white 6, cobalt .5) dry drags load .2, pressure .15–.35→.03; then a few round-5 pointed gestures of white near the lip. Blend mask's hard bottom showed as a box: hide under foam / soften more.
  - Pure white dry drags straight onto a solid wet dark = solid noodles; they only streak well after the gray veil+blend step.
  - Foam: scumble hand gives square blocky dabs; glaze hand with thinned white left a visible ellipse ring; soft round short arcs + horizontal blend = soft cloud but blobby edge. Still unresolved — try short horizontal round strokes over a soft mask, then blend, in the painting.
  - Background: graded piles glow→amber→deeprust with broad cov 3, clip, fill, then one blend pass = warm smooth gradient (good).
  - Foliage: deeprust body dabs + rust stipple w14 drag 5 + gold w12 + palegold w10, cluster, feather .5 = leafy cluster, but an elliptical mask reads as a blob. Use noise-shaped masks and varying coverage.
  - Birch: ribbon mask + body hand flat strokes = clean opaque trunk but a pipe (round ends, even width); dashes of lenticel = too neat. Need irregular edges, bigger broken dark marks, warm reflected light on shadow side.
- day 1, 18:40: Painting, day 1:
  - Background (campaign 1a): graded piles glow/haze/amber/deeprust/woods_dark by distance from a glow centre (400,330), broad hand cov 3, fill; blend angle .3 → warm gradient. Good.
  - FAILED: far trunks as flat-brush strokes of fartrunk (white 2, umber 1, red earth .4, smalt .8), load .6 = pale lavender poles, too light and regular. Rag (width 26, dip .7, pressure .55, path wipe) lifted almost nothing visible. Knife scrape (pressure 1, twice) took only the top; the trunk color stayed in the weave (value 166 vs bg 207).
  - REPAIR that worked: overpainted with the background's graded piles over ribbon masks (w+16), body hand cov 3.5, fill — the wet trunk paint mixed in and left darker soft columns; one vertical blend (angle pi/2+.1) over the whole background → misty woods with ghost trunks and light shafts. Better than the plan.
  - Rock band, pool base laid (rock/woods/deeprust; pool_dark/rock/woods/deeprust/amber). Rock band currently one flat dark: must be broken by falls, moss, stream.
- day 1, 19:31: Scratch trials 3 (rocks & moss, over wet rock/woods body fill):
  - Knife slabs of rocklite/rockwarm (load .6, pressure .25–.4) = flat pale planks; flat-12 dabs = scattered chips. Neither reads as rock.
  - form{} ellipsoid/block lit masks with body strokes = lumpy blobs; lit mask covers most of the form at front .4.
  - Hand-drawn facets (outline char broken) painted cov 3, fill, clip=true + blend inside = clean flat cutout planes (too diagrammatic), but they do read as planes.
  - Moss: stipple w10–12 of mossdark/moss = lichen dots; an offset band cap (A - A:offset(-28)) = even horseshoe (bad). mosslite (chrome 2, green earth 1, white 1, ochre .5) far too acid yellow as rim touches.
  - Hypothesis to test on the painting: moss = noise-shaped patches on the upper parts of rocks, round-9 body strokes of mossdark/moss + soft blend, then sparse lighter touches of a duller light (moss + glow), edges soft; rock faces dark with firm/soft varied edges, not clip.
- day 2, 06:14: Day 2 early: FAILED falls attempt. Glassy lip + gray streaks + blend read OK-ish (soft column) but a bell/box shape; then dark strand gestures and rock shapes laid over were too crisp and diagrammatic; light gestures on rock edges = noodles. Knife scrape (w30, pressure 1) over the wet stack left a crosshatch of weave; dipped rag (w40, dip .9, p .8, 2 passes each direction) lifted it to almost bare ground (a cream box). Repainted the box with rock/crevice/woods body cov 3 → a dark square block now waiting for the falls. Lesson: build the falls as ONE progressive passage in its own natural shape, not as a sheet then cut into with rocks; rocks first, water over them.
  Far banks attempt (farbank mixes, filbert dabs) = flat gray band; repainted with the background graded piles + vertical blend → misty band. Left a sliver of upper stream (lightened) behind the lip.
- day 2, 19:15: Scratch trials 4 (falls over wet rock dark):
  - Repaint test: rock+crevice body cov 3 load .9 over a wet gray curtain covers it back to dark (dipped rag lift first made no visible difference).
  - Separate flat-brush strands = noodles even after 2 blends (blend just smears them to smoky gray).
  - Fan 26 drags of fallwhite/fallgray load .3, pressure .5→.1, orient across = streaky water (good). thinwhite (white 8, ochre .2, cobalt .1, thinner .5) flat 12 strokes x3 passes = a fine gray hairy veil (good base).
  - RECIPE F (worked): lip band lipglass → thinwhite veil 3 passes → fan 24 drags (22) fallwhite/fallgray → one vertical blend over a soft rect → fan 20 light drags (9) fallwhite in the lit part → round 4 pointed accents. Reads as falling water.
  - DON'T: drag a wiped flat down out of the lip — it carried dark residue and printed a comb of dark teeth.
  - Rag path wipes with a 14-wide rag: face full after one wipe over thick wet paint.
- day 2, 20:04: Scratch trial 5 — BIRCH recipe that reads (over a setting amber background, ~26 h old):
  - birch (white 8, ochre .25, chrome .05), birch_mid (white 5, umber .4, ochre .3, smalt .4), birch_shadow2 (white 2, umber 1, smalt 1, bone black .25, cobalt .2), birch_warm (white 2, ochre 1, red earth .4, umber .4) for reflected light on the far edge.
  - Trunk mask = poly of axis ± w/2, :roughen(1.5, 12, seed); work body, flat 7, length 20–50, angle -pi/2, cov 3, fill, edge {found .7, soft .3}; graded piles by across-trunk u (lit left).
  - Marks: lenticel (bone black 1, umber 1.2), round 4 point .6, gestures pressure .2→.45–.8→.1 across 15–60% of width; chevron scars; base furrows. Reads as birch; marks a bit uniform — vary with grayer marks.
  - Setting background lets the trunk sit cleanly.
- day 3, 01:59: Day 3 01:59 — step back. Whole picture is static: canopy confetti band on top, empty glow, a uniform dark horizontal rock band with a gray rectangle of falls, dark pool. Birches float, ending on the band. Decisions:
  1. Restructure the middle into a V: wooded banks (mid-value warm undergrowth, lit crests facing the glow) rising from the falls to the sides — left to ~y440 at x0, right to ~y580 at x1000 — so the diagonals lead into the notch and the glow funnels onto the falls. Birch bases go on the right bank crest (covered by undergrowth at their feet).
  2. Canopy still open: merge the confetti into masses, keep holes, then fewer accents.
  3. Pool is tacky in places: wait till dry, then repaint it as one fresh wet passage (base → vertical reflection pulls → horizontal blend).
  4. Falls: shape the lip, widen downward, foam/mist at base.
  Rock steps (worley/flat): stratified ledge reads but is too heavy.

Autumn woodland stream: a small waterfall over a mossy ledge into a pool, white birches, gold/rust foliage, backlit glow in the woods behind the falls (upper left-centre). Wet-on-wet; most of the middle band is still open, the background is setting, the pool (bottom third) is tacky/dry and I plan to repaint it entirely as one fresh wet passage with vertical reflections of the canopy, birches and falls. I know the middle reads as a horizontal stage set (striped ledges, rectangular falls, brown bar above the lip). What would you change first in the large masses and value structure before I build detail?

content.thinking:
I'm picturing the composition as a portrait: canopy masses forming an arch framing a glow at the upper left-center, with two near-vertical birches on the right trailing brown drip tags. Below that, I'm envisioning a middle band of horizontal moss ledges spanning the width, interrupted by a knife-textured brown slab.

The waterfall itself sits as a rectangle flanked by two rounded lime-green moss bushes at its base, with a golden-rust undergrowth mound rising on the left bank. Below, the pool splits into a dark-gray upper half and warm orange lower half with leaf-shaped silhouettes, and I'm checking whether this reflects the logic of what's above it—near water should mirror sky, far water should mirror the banks, so the gold-rust bottom and dark-gray top actually track correctly, though the hard horizontal split between them needs softening. In terms of value, the glow, birches, and falls read lightest, while the middle band and pool top sit at a uniform mid-dark.

The real structural issue is the horizontals: the ledge stripes, brown bar, and straight rock-band edge at y~900 all cut across the canvas and conflict with the verticals of the falls rectangle and twin birches, forming an unwanted grid. The composition wants a V shape where the banks rise from the falls outward to the sides—the left mound already does this, and the right has a lower lit undergrowth—but the full-width striped ledges at y~620-780 slice straight across and undermine that V, so that's the first thing I'd fix in the big masses.

I also need to sort out the value hierarchy: right now the darkest darks are scattered rather than flanking the falls, and the falls themselves read as mid-gray instead of the brightest light below the backlit glow, with a mid-value brown bar awkwardly sitting between the two.

Thinking further about the lighting logic, since the glow is backlighting the falls, the lip should catch and transmit gold light while the face stays darker with streak highlights, and critically the pool should mirror that glow below the rock band — a reflection I'm currently missing.

It doesn't need to be strictly optical, though — the real fix is turning the pool's dead dark band into a vertical light path connecting glow, falls, and foam down toward the viewer, which transforms the horizontal composition into a vertical cascade of light. I'm also noting the dark leaf-like shapes at bottom-left might actually be the left canopy's scalloped edge reflected.

The brown mushroom-cap bar above the lip also needs replacing — it should instead be a narrow, backlit stream surface flowing between converging dark banks toward the misty distance, with the lip rendered as a bright line, and the pale misty zone between the bar and the glow treated with vertical streaks.

The two birches at the edges look pasted on rather than grounded — same width, lean, and spacing, both clipped at the top and tagged with a brown drip at their base. Their bases need an actual bank to stand on, and under this backlighting their lit sides should face toward the glow.

So the real answer should address sequencing of moves. I'm also noticing the canopy's symmetrical arch framing feels theatrical and proscenium-like, with hard cauliflower edges where they meet the glow — backlit foliage should instead have broken, lost edges with sky holes letting the glow bleed through, not a crisp uniform silhouette.

Priority order emerges: break that hard perimeter line with sky holes, and push a real value gradient across the canopy mass — darker underneath, warmer and lighter where it meets the glow — rather than uniform mid-tone flatness with scattered confetti specks. But the very first move should be rebuilding the middle band: reshape the banks into a V, killing the full-width stripes and that straight bottom edge.

I need to verify the V geometry against the falls position (center ~480), the glow at ~400, and the birches at 780/930 — a rise from y~440 on the left to y~580 on the right seems to work given the existing golden mound and the low undergrowth on the right. The falls themselves also need fixing: right now they're a flat rectangle with straight sides, equal-width top and bottom, three uniform white streaks, and no foam where they hit the waterline — that's the next problem to solve.

Those bushes read too much like a formal garden's matching hedges, which fights the naturalistic intent — the acid chroma and rounded topiary shape are the real problems, not just the moss concept underneath. I'm trying to eyeball the value ladder across the scene: glow near 220, canopy 120-140, birches 235, ledge band 80-110, pool graduating down from around 75.

Squinting at it, I see the light forms a vertical spine from glow down through the scene, but it gets cut twice — once by the mid-tone brown bar and again by the dark pool beneath the falls. Reconnecting that light path is the real fix, and since the brown bar sits in the still-wet middle band, that's the place to address first, before the pool dries tacky.

Since the painter can repaint wet sections with body color, I'm sequencing the work: resolve the middle band (banks, V-shape, upper stream, lip) first, then the falls shape and foam, then the pool last — since reflections need the middle settled before they're convincing. Now I'm mapping out concretely where the left bank's gold undergrowth slopes down toward the lip and what replaces the horizontal stripes beneath it.

I'm realizing the pool's far edge shouldn't read as a flat line — the plan called for a mossy foreground rock at lower-left that juts into the pool, breaking the horizontal and adding depth, which is currently missing. I'm also noting the darkest values belong on the wet rock flanking the falls and tucked under the lip, per the original plan.

The band currently spreads its darkest darks too evenly — I should concentrate the deepest value right beside the falls, especially the right side, letting it lighten and warm toward the banks where lit crests catch the glow, which is already the plan's intent. To break the stripy look I need to repaint with diagonal masses rather than flat bands, using graded piles and blending instead of uniform strokes.

Mapping canvas coordinates: the rust drips at the birch bases sit around y 664-718, with trunks at roughly x 785-830 and 902-936. The right bank's crest should rise near y 650-700 where undergrowth hides the birch roots, so I'm widening the trunk base slightly as it disappears into that lit gold undergrowth.

I also notice both birches currently end at the same height with similar widths, making them read as if on the same plane — I'd rather stagger their base heights and vary trunk width so one reads as nearer and the other farther back, and check that their leans aren't too parallel, since right now they converge upward in a similar direction rather than feeling like distinct trees in space.

Actually, checking the trunk lines more carefully, the left birch leans toward the top-left and the right one leans toward the top-right, so they actually diverge upward into a V shape rather than staying parallel — that reads well and echoes the composition's larger V motif. I'm also thinking about value contrast: the birches are the brightest whites in the piece, brighter even than the falls, but under contre-jour lighting they should mostly sit in shadow with just a lit rim catching the glow — worth checking whether the lit side of each trunk matches the direction of that background glow.

That bright trunk-against-canopy contrast will pull the eye off the top of the frame, so I'd dim the trunks a step below the falls' lights. The canopy edges against the glow are scalloped and continuous, and under backlight those edges should read as broken, warm light leaking through with sky holes within the masses rather than solid silhouettes.

Also I notice the left canopy has no trunk holding it up — it reads as a floating cloud of leaves, while the right canopy has support since the birches rise directly into it. Adding a dark trunk or two climbing from the left bank into the left canopy would fix that and also give a nice contre-jour silhouette balancing the white birches on the right.

Stepping back to priorities: if asked what to fix first in the large masses before adding detail, my answer would be the middle band — the flat stripes and straight edges need to go. I'd replace them with diagonal bank masses rising in a V, turn the brown bar into a bright glowing stream receding toward the falls, concentrate the darkest values on the rocks flanking the falls and under the lip, and lighten outward toward the lit crests.

Beyond that: break the waterline so it's not a flat edge, vary bank toes and foreground rocks at different heights, dull and break the symmetry of the lime bushes, shape and foam the falls' base with warm light at the lip, and keep the pool as one passage with a light vertical reflection path under the falls flanked by darker bank reflections — avoiding any horizontal light/dark split. The birches and canopy edges come after. content.text:
I'd start with the notch: the brown bar, the ghost curtain above it, and the rock tight against the falls. The order and reasons are below. Coordinates are in canvas units (1000 × 1250).

**What the picture is doing now**

You've named the stage set yourself, so I'll just add what I counted. From top to bottom there are about eight stacked horizontals:
- the left canopy's underside (~y330)
- the top of the ghost curtain (~y475)
- the top and bottom of the brown bar (y615 / y675)
- three or four ledge stripes (y630–765), running edge to edge at even spacing with the same values on both sides of the falls
- the tops of the two bushes
- a dead-straight waterline at y900 across the full width
- the dark/orange split in the pool (~y1070)

Everything sits in a layer parallel to the picture plane and nothing overlaps anything, so there's no depth. The falls are a pasted-on plate: straight sides, flat top and bottom, three evenly spaced streaks, ending exactly on the waterline.

On values, the problem I'd rank above all the horizontals is this: **the chain of light is cut twice.** The glow (brightest around x400–450, y250–330) should flow down into the lip, the falls, the foam and the falls' reflection. That vertical is your picture. Right now the brown bar (a mid-value slab) cuts it between the glow and the falls, and the dark top of the pool cuts it below the falls. In squint you get a bright hole at the top, a dark band and a gray rectangle, and no connection between them.

**The governing idea: commit to contre-jour**

The light comes from behind, so whatever faces us should be in shadow and the lights should be rims. At the moment several passages are lit from the front:
- The lime bushes (x245–380 and x595–825, y770–900) are lit on their faces, at the highest chroma in the middle band. They also bracket the falls like a pair of hedges at a fountain.
- The ledge stripes have light olive bands on their fronts.
- The birches are lit across about 60% of their width and are the lightest, crispest values in the picture. They're lighter than the glow and pull the eye to the right edge and off the top.

Under backlight the faces of the banks are a warm mid-dark. The light sits only on crest edges, moss tops and the trunks' glow-side rims. The lip of the falls is where the light comes through the water, so it should be the brightest note below the glow. If the whole picture obeys this, the glow gets its power and the falls become the focus.

**What I'd take up first: the notch (x250–700, y470–700)**

Do this while it's open, because the V, the lip and the falls' width all hang from it.
1. **Kill the brown bar over the falls.** At this eye level the upper stream is nearly edge-on, so the lip is a thin, warm, bright sliver (10–15 units, not 60), uneven along its length.
2. **Reuse the bar's ends.** Its overhangs (x300–380 and x585–670) can become the shoulders of the flanking rocks, darkened, with their tops at different heights, overlapping the ends of the lip. The relief view shows the knife crust is thick. Scrape it down where light paint has to go, or that pebble texture will show through the lip.
3. **Put the darkest darks of the whole picture here**, on the wet rock hard against both sides of the falls and just under the lip. Let one or two rock edges come in front of the falls' edges so the water sits behind the rock and not on top of it.
4. **Above the lip, lose the ghost curtain's top edge** (y475, with the little brown hook at about x265) into the glow. Its darker left end (x255–330) could stay as a far trunk in mist. The misty woods should come straight down to the lip, a little darker at the flanks, without their own top edge.

**Second: the V, which replaces the stripes**

Your left crest is already there: the gold mound falls from about (0,430) to about (330,600). The right crest is the lit undergrowth at y570–660. What's missing is the bank mass under those crests following the diagonal. Instead, a striped rectangle fills it.

Paint the banks as diagonal masses with the graded body fill that worked for your background, but grade by distance from the falls rather than from the glow: darkest at the notch, warming and lightening toward the outer ends, with light only on the crest rims. That way the value structure comes out of the method.

Make the two arms unequal. Left: higher and steeper. Right: lower, longer and broken by the birches. The V and the canopy arch together could otherwise make a symmetrical hourglass around the glow.

Break the y900 waterline into steps: the bank toes enter the water at different heights. Bring in the mossy foreground rock at lower left from your plan, overlapping both the bank and the pool. It's the one form that can come in front of the falls and give the space a near plane.

Moss goes as dull, uneven patches on rock tops, with light only on top edges. Don't make it two symmetrical lime humps.

**Then, in order**
- **Falls:** widen them downward, make the edges ragged, and keep the lights warm near the lip. Let the foam break the bottom edge and spill over the waterline so the falls stop landing exactly on it.
- **Pool:** paint it as one passage, as you planned. Lay a vertical light path under the falls (falls plus foam plus, lower down, the glow reflected a step darker than the glow itself), with the banks' darker reflections on either side. No horizontal split across the full width. The current y1070 boundary and the navy cutout shapes go.
- **Birches:** lower the faces by a step to a warm or cool light-mid gray. Keep a thin bright rim on the glow side and soften the edges where they cross the haze. Their bases end in identical rust drips at the same height (y665–720) and look pinned on. Plant them at different heights inside the right-bank undergrowth, with the undergrowth painted over their feet.
- **Canopy:** the inner edge against the glow is one continuous hard scalloped line, which shows clearly in the edges view. In backlight that edge is where the leaves are most translucent. Lose it in places, open sky holes in the masses, and darken toward the outer corners. The left mass also floats: one dark trunk under it, against the haze around x100–150, would hold it up and give the left side a backlit silhouette to answer the white birches.

So the first move is the notch: the bar, the curtain's edge, and the darkest rock against the falls. Once the glow, lip and falls connect, the V has a place to converge on and the pool has something to reflect.
